prompt.context: Our client owns a designer shoe store that makes high-end, made-to-measure shoes for customers. The high-quality product has gained popularity rapidly and the client wants to ramp up production. However, the highly-skilled labor that the client employs is hard to come by.
prompt.question: Our client wants us to help them figure out how to increase output without adversely affecting quality and the company's potential profitability.

clarifying_info.q: Are there additional skilled shoemakers available in the market?
clarifying_info.a: No, there are no additional skilled shoemakers available in the market.

clarifying_info.q: How many workers does the client currently employ?
clarifying_info.a: There are 15 workers. Each worker currently takes an average of 12 hours to produce one pair of shoes.

clarifying_info.q: What does the shoe-making process look like?
clarifying_info.a: The process has 3 stages: cutting, stitching, and finishing. Currently, each shoemaker performs all three steps.

clarifying_info.q: Can the process be changed so that shoemakers perform specific tasks (specialization)?
How many hours do employees work?
clarifying_info.a: Employees work 9 hours a day, 5 days a week.

clarifying_info.q: What are the economics — price, costs, wages?
clarifying_info.a: Selling price: $300/pair. Material cost: $40/pair. Shipping: $10/pair. Employee wages: $15/hour. Fixed costs: $1,000/week.

exhibits.title: Employee Survey — Hours per Activity by Group
exhibits.shows: A table showing the results of an employee survey. The 15 workers are divided into three groups of 5. For each group, the table lists the number of hours that group takes to complete each of the three tasks (cutting, stitching, finishing) and the total hours per pair.

framework: Understand the current production process end-to-end (steps, time, labor allocation)
Identify constraints: no new skilled labor can be hired
Explore internal levers: can labor be redeployed or specialized?
Quantify the impact of specialization on output (time per pair reduced)
Calculate new weekly output under the optimized process
Calculate profitability: revenue, variable costs, labor costs, fixed costs, net profit
Identify risks and next steps for implementation

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1, how should the client restructure the workforce to maximize output, and why?
questions.guidance: The candidate should identify that each group has one task it completes in 3 hours — the minimum possible. By assigning each group to its fastest task exclusively, the total hours per pair drops from 12 to 9. Group 1 should specialize in Cutting (3 hrs), Group 3 in Stitching (3 hrs), and Group 2 in Finishing (3 hrs). This is pure specialization / division-of-labor logic. The candidate should explicitly state the new average time per pair = 9 hours.

questions.prompt: Under the new specialized process, what is the maximum weekly output for the entire workforce?
questions.guidance: The candidate should use: hours per week per employee, new hours per pair, and total headcount to derive weekly pairs produced.

math.setup: Each employee works 9 hrs/day x 5 days = 45 hrs/week. Under the new system, the bottleneck time per pair is 9 hours (3 hrs cutting + 3 hrs stitching + 3 hrs finishing, each done by a specialist group of 5). Output per employee = 45 / 9 = 5 pairs/week. Total output = 5 pairs x 15 employees = 75 pairs/week.
steps: Hours per week per employee = 9 hrs/day x 5 days = 45 hrs
Output per employee per week = 45 hrs / 9 hrs per pair = 5 pairs
Total weekly output = 5 pairs x 15 employees = 75 pairs

questions.prompt: What is the client's weekly and annual profit under the new system?
questions.guidance: The candidate should build a simple P&L: gross profit per pair, total gross profit, subtract labor cost (wage x total hours worked), subtract fixed costs. Should ask for price, costs, and wages if not already given.

math.setup: Revenue: $300/pair. Variable costs per pair: $40 (materials) + $10 (shipping) = $50. Labor cost = 15 employees x 45 hrs/week x $15/hr. Fixed costs = $1,000/week. Weekly output = 75 pairs.
steps: Total gross profit per week = $250 x 75 pairs = $18,750
Total employee cost per week = 15 employees x 45 hrs x $15/hr = $10,125

recommendation: Restructure the workforce into three specialized groups, each focused on a single production task: Group 1 on cutting, Group 3 on stitching, Group 2 on finishing.

This specialization reduces average production time per pair from 12 hours to 9 hours, enabling a weekly output of 75 pairs with the existing 15 employees — a 33% increase in output with no additional hiring.
Under this model, the business generates approximately $7,625 in weekly profit and ~$396,500 annually.
risks: Employees accustomed to performing all three tasks may resist the transition to a specialized role, creating implementation friction.
Any heavily entrenched process change carries execution risk; disruptions during the transition could temporarily reduce output or quality.
Layout changes in the workshop to support a production-line model may incur one-time setup costs.
Over-specialization could reduce workforce flexibility if one group is absent or unavailable.
next_steps: Pilot the specialized workflow with one sub-group first to validate time savings and surface any quality or morale issues before full rollout.
Implement the change in a phased manner to minimize disruption while capturing gains progressively.
Monitor output and quality metrics closely in the first weeks post-implementation to catch problems early.
Assess whether the workshop layout needs to be reconfigured to support a sequential production-line flow.
